title: Prachi Mishra of Goldman Sachs' Chief India Economist On FY21 GDP | Exclusive
description: Goldman Sachs warns India GDP may fall to a multi-decade low of sub 2% in FY21. Watch the Exclusive chat with Goldman Sachs Chief India Economist Prachi Mishra with ET Now. asr.full_text: The Chief Economist of Goldman Sachs here in India, Prachi Mishra. She came out with the note recently last evening, in fact, warning that the growth in India could fall to multi-decade lows. Now, Prachi, very good afternoon to you and thank you very much for taking time out for us today and coming on the show. Very interesting note, one of the most cautioning and warning notes we have really read in recent times which makes the case that the growth may fall sub 2%. What are the indicators you are looking at which have turned green to amber or even perhaps red, which is leading to that kind of a dire forecast. Thank you. Thank you, AJ. Pleasure to talk to you. Let me get started, perhaps, with our outlook for the global economy because that's a important input for our forecast for the Indian economy. Let's flash back a little. Earlier during the year, we were relatively optimistic about the Indian economy. So let it be flashback a little bit. You know, earlier during the year, we were relatively optimistic about the global economy. Our global growth forecast for 2020 was three point two five percent. And our view was that, you know, the global economy would be better in 2020, supported by easier financial conditions. And to U.S.-China trade war escalation since then however our global view has changed completely we've revised our global growth projections down sharply by more than five% relative to a pre-virus situation so our current global growth forecast for 2020 is minus 2% and just to give you our sense of what the numbers look like for particular countries, for the United States and for the Euro area, we have minus 6% and minus 9% respectively for 2020. And if you look at quarterly numbers for the United States, we have a forecast of a 34% contraction in the level of real output in Q2 of 2020. So then let me then come to India based on what the global economy would look like. And, um, and, and let me say that on, on India, relative to, um, you know, early March. When the buyers situation was fairly benign in India, we have revised our growth forecast dramatically. We, you know, March when the virus situation was fairly benign in India we have revised our growth forecasts dramatically we you know pre virus our forecast was closer to 6% in fact 5.8% for fiscal year 2021 which is the fiscal year from April 2020 to March 21 now we are at 1.6%, as you pointed out as well. This is a gigantic 420 basis point downgrade. Exaborate a bit on, three key reasons for this sharp downgrade compared to the pre-virus situation. Number one, I think given that, as I said, we have revised our global growth projections down by more than a five percentage point relative to a previous situation. This would definitely have implications for India growth. And using elasticities of how much India growth would react to global growth using historical data that should be bestimated. This would be roughly one-fifty basis point down grade for India growth. Number two, what these forecast these forecasts do suggest is, is they take into account directly the effect of the lockdown. So currently, we are in week three. We are basically assuming 25% of the activity would be wiped out in these three weeks. And in addition, we're assuming, as seems to be the case now, that there would be a staggered exit from the lockdown, as seems to be the case now, that there would be a staggered exit from the lockdown, as seems to be the recent thinking. So this, if you take into account the fact that 25, at least 25 percent of the activity would be wiped out during these three weeks, and in addition, some sort of a staggered exit from the lockdown, this would amount to roughly around a 220 basis- point reduction in growth. And number three, the account for some additional spillover effects on investment. Prashi, let me just interrupt you just a bit over there. Just we'll take those points bit by bit. Let's break it up. Let's go back to that point which you were making that this comes in a global backdrop of economic activity shrinking. Before we could break those points up, I would like to know the 2 biggest engines in global growth so far in your view or your numbers are showing which is US and China. How badly are they hit and what do you see are the roadmap for them recovering? Because we would be following that route as well. Then we'll come to India factors Sure. Sure, Ajay. As I said for the United States, in annual average terms, we have a forecast of minus 6 percent. And in fact, in Q2, just think about these numbers, you know, 34% contraction in real activity in the U.S., in Q2. So these are huge numbers. Similarly, I think across most countries, we actually have sharp quarterly contractions, quarter and quarter reduction in the level of real GDP in both Q1 and Q2. Sure. Okay. Lets come back Prachy to analyse the policy-action. We know this is unprecedented economic challenges which the world faces and we cannot be immune to this. How have you analyzed the policy measures and the global central banks kind of, what kind of room do they have because this is originally a health crisis which is blowing up into an economic crisis. How have you analyzed or compared China's actions, U.S. central banks and policy makers, and how do we as a country stack, though we have just rolled out half of it, some more is expected? Right. Ajay, as you correctly pointed out, this is truly an unprecedented shock, globally and for the Indian economy, and if you think about it, one key difference vis-a-vis some of the earlier episodes is this whole fear and scare factor among citizens around the world was clearly not not prevalent at all in any of the previous recession episodes. Now the covid-19 crisis, a more precise response to that crisis now what were you dealing with that crisis you're basically imposing lockdown social distancing this. The response to the crisis represents a physical constraint on economic activity which is different from see a financial prices being. There's a shock to the financial sector This kind of a shock is truly unprecedented in post war history And whenever the constraint is physical, you actually see sharp contractions in economic activity which you are seeing across the world and we forecast it to be the same in Q2 as well And now come to your question on you know policy responses you know given that the shock is unprecedented policy responses need to be unprecedented too and you know the first this is a global health pandemic so the first line of defense has to be to contain the spread of the virus and to deal with the infected population and if you come to india now you know both the center and the virus and to deal with the infected population and if you come to India now you'll both the centre and the state governments have been fairly proactive from the start and taken a number of steps in terms of screening people closing borders the nationwide lockdowns since March 24th and which is likely to exit most likely in staggered fashions and going forward we expect more measures to come. See macro economic policy whether it's fiscal policy, monetary policy in a crisis like this, it can only be a second line of defense. If you come to monetary policy, of course, you know, global central banks, but even in India, you know, the RBI has stopped interest rates by 75 basis points ahead of the schedule MPC need and has taken a number of liquidity infusion measures. We do expect that going forward there would be more rate reductions, especially we have bought in 50 basis points more by the end of Q3. And this is due to three main reasons if you look at the Central Bank's response. Number one, I think headline inflation is likely to come down. Number two, I think risks to our growth forecast. Despite these sharp downgrades, actually remain to the downside. And third, if you look at the RBI's forward guidance provided during the governor's press briefing last time, it does suggest space for further action, as well. So let me come to the second pillar of macroeconomic policy, which is fiscal policy, and there, I think, a lot of discussion that India does not have much fiscal space, how much fiscal response should be there. And there, I think we've been saying this for a while. Clearly I think if you look at public sector deficit net of assets sales, for India, it's close to 10% of GDP and it remains the highest among emerging economies. So no question about that. What is important to note however, at this point, that these are more medium to long term arguments. Right now the economy is facing a globally unprecedented shock. And the lack of fiscal space perhaps implies that answers your question as well. India perhaps cannot have a fiscal response of 10 to 15% of GDP like many, many advanced economies have done. However, I think what I would like to stress in the Indian context is that rather than focusing on sheer magnitudes, I think what market participants are looking for is more you know, whether the fiscal response is temporary, it's targeted, whether it's carefully calibrated and it's properly executed. Prachi, you know, this is also a time that almost everybody is going back to their textbook, going back to the economic history and trying to find out how have economics, worldwide, you know, come back from deep recession. What does your study say, how exactly does it happen, how much does Rebuilding of shaken structures of economy actually take? How do large corporates and economy work together? Give us some instances. What exactly the model of rebuilding the world or even India? Look, Ajay, let me say that each economist's experience is different. Depending on what the initial conditions were. Depending on how the institutional structure is. In this case, how the public health system is. So I think it's not apples and apples to compare across economies, because they differ in a number of ways. The policy responses differ, the thinking differs. What I can say here is that in the case of India, the average of 1.6%, which you might think that it's a really low number, actually assumes a strong sequential recovery in the second half of the fiscal year. And this is based basically on three assumptions. Number one, I think that three-week-nation lockdown, which is expected to be removed rather sequentially and social distancing measures actually reduce new infections over the next four to six weeks. Number two, I think while the fiscal easing so far has been limited, our expectation, and so is the market expectation of further fiscal stimulus by the central government as well as the states, I think a package for the small and medium corporates, for example, is under discussion. And number three, I think for the central bank to continue with its monetary easing policy along with liquidity infusion measures. So just to summarize and to be clear, 1.6% looks a really low number and in fact is one of the deepest if you compare to India's previous quote-unquote recession episodes, but remember that given the in Q1 and Q q2 given that you are going to have a contraction in output in q1 and q2 of this year a number a number like 1.6 percent would actually require a strong sequential recovery in the second half of the fiscal year video.

The Chief Economist of Goldman Sachs here in India, Prachi Mishra. She came out with the note recently last evening, in fact, warning that the growth in India could fall to multi-decade lows. Now, Prachi, very good afternoon to you and thank you very much for taking time out for us today and coming on the show. Earlier during the year, we were relatively optimistic about the Indian economy. So let it be flashback a little bit. You know, earlier during the year, we were relatively optimistic about the global economy. Our global growth forecast for 2020 was three point two five percent. United States and for the Euro area, we have minus 6% and minus 9% respectively for 2020. We, you know, March when the virus situation was fairly benign in India we have revised our growth forecasts dramatically we you know pre virus our forecast was closer to 6% in fact 5.8% for fiscal year 2021 which is the fiscal year from April 2020 to March 21 now we are at 1.6%, as you pointed out as well. This is a gigantic 420 basis point downgrade. Exaborate a bit on, three key reasons for this sharp downgrade compared to the pre-virus situation. Number one, I think given that, as I said, we have revised our global growth projections down by more than a five percentage point relative to a previous situation. This would definitely have implications for India growth. And using elasticities of how much India growth would react to global growth using historical data that should be bestimated. This would be roughly one-fifty basis point down grade for India growth. Number two, what these forecast these forecasts do suggest is, is they take into account directly the effect of the lockdown. So currently, we are in week three. We are basically assuming 25% of the activity

would be wiped out in these three weeks. And in addition, we're assuming, as seems to be the case now, that there would be a staggered exit from the lockdown, as seems to be the case now, that there would be a staggered exit from the lockdown, as seems to be the recent thinking. So this, if you take into account the fact that 25, at least 25 percent of the activity would be wiped out during these three weeks, and in addition, some sort of a staggered exit from the lockdown, this would amount to roughly around a 220 basis- point reduction in growth. And number three, the account for some additional spillover effects on investment. Prashi, let me just interrupt you just a bit over there. Just we'll take those points bit by bit. Let's break it up. Let's go back to that point which you were making that this comes in a global backdrop of economic activity shrinking. Before we could break those points up, I would like to know the 2 biggest engines in global growth so far in your view or your numbers are showing which is US and China. How badly are they hit and what do you see are the roadmap for them recovering? Because we would be following that route as well. Then we'll come to India factors Sure. Sure, Ajay. As I said for the United States, in annual average terms, we have a forecast of minus 6 percent. And in fact, in Q2, just think about these numbers, you know, 34% contraction in real activity in the U.S., in Q2. So these are huge numbers. Similarly, I think across most countries, we actually have sharp quarterly contractions, quarter and quarter reduction in the level of

real GDP in both Q1 and Q2. Sure. Okay. Lets come back Prachy to analyse the policy-action. We know this is unprecedented economic challenges which the world faces and we cannot be immune to this. Now the covid-19 crisis, a more precise response to that crisis now what were you dealing with that crisis you're basically imposing lockdown social distancing this. The response to the crisis represents a physical constraint on economic activity which is different from see a financial prices being. We do expect that going forward there would be more rate reductions, especially we have bought in 50 basis points more by the end of Q3. And this is due to three main reasons if you look at the Central Bank's response. Number one, I think headline inflation is likely to come down. Number two, I think risks to our growth forecast. Despite these sharp downgrades, actually remain to the downside. And third, if you look at the RBI's forward guidance provided during the governor's press briefing last time, it does
